items.originalTitle: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.author: Will Steakin
items.title: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.summary: Ro Khanna hasn't launched a 2028 bid yet, but he already has a pioneer of the populist left in his corner. Progressive firebrand Cenk Uygur is set to formally endorse the California Democrat on Thursday night during his annual appearance on nephew Hasan Piker's Twitch stream, a Thanksgiving Day debate-a-thon the pair call "Cenksgiving." Uygur told POLITICO he will pitch Khanna as the best populist progressive candidate. His Rebellion PAC will also debut its first 2028 ad promoting a Khanna candidacy Thursday night. "For me, it's a no-brainer," Uygur said in an interview, explaining why he’s backing Khanna. "Who else would you back, and why would any progressive or any populist back anyone else?" Along with his PAC getting behind Khanna, Uygur is also launching his own "Draft Ro" website to collect signatures and showcase other early high-profile endorsers, though he wouldn't say who just yet. The endorsement is one of the first of the 2028 cycle, and it comes before any major candidate has formally announced. Inside Washington, Khanna’s chances are viewed as quite slim. But for Uygur, that kind of underestimation is exactly part of the draw. "I love it," Uygur said of the skepticism. "I wouldn't have backed him if anyone in D.C. was behind him." "We're running against Washington," he added. "So if Washington doesn't like a candidate, perfect." Uygur is pairing his endorsement with a litmus test he’s trying to lay down for 2028 progressives: Candidates must call what Israel has done in Gaza a genocide and support ending U.S. funding for Israel. "It isn't actually about Israel," Uygur said. "It's about: Is this person going to represent us or not?" Khanna, he said, is "among the very, very few, and maybe the only candidate, that'll pass that test." He allowed for one other: "There's also AOC. If she runs, that's another person that could pass the test." But that's as far as the praise goes. His endorsement of Khanna comes as many other progressives are waiting to see whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) jumps in. Uygur isn't one of them. Asked if her entry would change his calculus, he said: "Not 1%." "Sorry, but I don't think AOC means it," he said. "I don't think she would do any of the things that she says, and so I'm not going to back someone who is not going to deliver." "She's obsessed with the establishment, so she's going to run a soft, weak race," he added. "She wants to make Democratic leaders and mainstream media happy. Good luck with that strategy." Khanna has told POLITICO he plans to decide whether to run after the holidays and that whether Ocasio-Cortez gets in won't factor into his decision. Uygur's backing could give the potential 2028 candidate some credibility on the populist left, not to mention a boost from "The Young Turks," one of the longest-running and most popular progressive shows online, which Uygur launched in 2002. He also co-founded Justice Democrats in 2017 and ran a long-shot bid of his own for the 2024 Democratic presidential nomination. His Rebellion PAC sparked controversy during the 2026 midterms with an ad tying U.S. funding for Israel to higher grocery prices, which the campaign of then-Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced itself from. Uygur, who was also a prominent backer of Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential runs, has a blunt prediction for 2028: "I'm positive Ro Khanna is going to win."

Sounding uncharacteristically relaxed, opening single Continuation is a woozier take on their often grinding approach to repetition, building into blissful contentment rather than rabid euphoria. “It’s gonna be fun,” Void exhales. “It’s gonna be … easy.” This third album takes in Factory Floor’s favoured influences – brain-spinning industrial noise, eccentric acid techno, a Kraftwerkian clarity of purpose – and bathes them in a warmer light. But that’s not to say they’ve softened. Standout track Buzz Saw has the album’s toughest synth line, serrated and stomping, for what should be a new live classic.

items.originalTitle: Data centers flood Black communities without residents having a say
items.author: Adam Mahoney, Capital B
items.title: Data centers flood Black communities without residents having a say
items.summary: Data centers have become a target for both Republican and Democratic campaign ads in the 2026 election. " data-large-file="https://wpln.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2026/10/Per-NPR-voters-are-fed-up-with-data-centers-and-campaigns-are-trying-to-cash-in-for-2026-elections-1024x576.jpg" /> By the time Zakiya Mabery learned that a $2 billion data center was planned just a 10-minute walk from her house, officials had already approved it. The 200-acre facility in Augusta, Georgia, was first authorized in 2022 without a public hearing that would’ve allowed the community to voice their concerns. Just months before the facility known as Project Eisenhower came to be, Mabery bought her home in a new housing development called Hayne’s Station. Since then, two-thirds of the people who’ve moved into the community have been Black. “We would’ve never purchased a house if we knew a data center was coming,” she said about the project that began construction earlier this year. Mabery’s experience exposes the racial divide in America’s data center boom — not just in where facilities are built, but in who gets a chance to question them. Majority-Black communities are more than two times more likely to host a data center than majority-white ones and far less likely to receive the chance to hear about the projects before they’re approved or offer their opinion through public comment. “It seems like (processes) are being built to silence citizens,” Mabery said at an Augusta Planning Commission meeting this past summer. In recent years, dozens of AI data centers in communities home to hundreds of thousands of Americans have been approved without a public hearing. This Is Nashville: Connecting the dots as data centers come to town For Black communities, the data center boom is extending a familiar pattern of environmental racism that has plagued families for generations. Black communities are hosting infrastructure that generates wealth elsewhere. Meanwhile, they live with the pollution and disinvestment that undermines economic opportunity and contributes to poor health outcomes and premature deaths in their neighborhoods. The stakes are growing as tech companies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into new infrastructure. President Donald Trump has pulled the levers of government in favor of these companies as he’s cast AI dominance as a competition the United States cannot afford to lose to China. His administration has ordered agencies to exempt data centers projects from federal environmental review and to revise federal rules to accelerate their construction. At the same time, he has pushed federal agencies to limit the opportunities for public comment as the building boom reaches communities already carrying generations of industrial burdens. The opportunity for residents to speak their mind is consequential to the outcome of a data center project. On average, communities that have received a hearing before construction are nearly 80% white on average. Those without one are roughly 60% people of color. When communities have received a public hearing, data centers have been blocked 66% of the time. When they don’t, they’re approved 80% of the time, according to Zoned Out, a tool created by researchers at Harvard University. “We know disparities already exist in our communities, and now in the case of data centers, we’re seeing the targeting that happens without any say. It is systemic injustice,” said Aino Halonen, a former AI worker who led the Harvard study. The racial disparities showed up during November’s midterm election. More than 40 jurisdictions nationwide allowed voters to decide if they wanted data centers in their communities via ballot measures. White residents made up an average of over 83% of the population in these places, compared with less than 5% for Black residents. The racial divide behind the data center boom In Georgia, Mabery and her neighbors want a voice in what happens to their homes, health, and finances. Data centers have increased PM 2.5 air pollution, which Black Americans die from at the highest rate in the U.S. The pollution can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer. Carbon emissions from data centers are also connected to the intensification of climate change. America’s largest data centers are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of climate change-causing carbon dioxide emissions annually — more than emissions from entire countries like Kenya and Guatemala. “These are not emotional concerns. This is where we live. We invested here. We live and bear the impact here,” Augusta resident Charles Zabel said about the data center. “We ought to have a voice in this. So far, we have not had a meaningful voice in this discussion. Representation does not mean protecting a project. Representation means protecting the people who already call this place home.” Noise pollution from data centers is coming. The gas-powered xAI model is spreading Researchers at George Washington University Law School joined American University researchers to analyze the placement of more than 5,200 data centers in the U.S., finding the major racial divide in where they’re found. Researchers accounted for income, population density, home values, and proximity to major power lines, and compared neighborhoods within the same state to test whether economics or geography explained the racial disparities in where data centers were located and the benefits the communities received. Even after those adjustments, neighborhoods with larger Black, Latino, and Asian populations remained most likely to have these negative experiences with data centers. “Even when you control for all of that, race stands out,” said Dhanaraj Thakur, director of the Fair Technology Initiative at George Washington University. “I think it’s important to show that this is not some anecdotal thing that’s happening in a few cities like Memphis or elsewhere,” he added. “It’s actually happening across the country.” The difference often comes down to zoning. Due to the long tentacles of segregation and redlining, Black people are far more likely to live in communities that are home to tracts zoned for industrial use. When a data center requires rezoning from, say, commercial to industrial, the approval process generally includes public notice, a hearing, and a vote. But if the land is already zoned industrial, developers can secure permits through an administrative review without requiring opportunities for residents to intervene. As Capital B has reported, there have been several incidents where developers have pursued projects in poorer, majority-Black neighborhoods with more lax public hearing requirements after encountering opposition in wealthier, whiter areas. After a data center was proposed in a wealthy, 65% white community in North Carolina, for example, thousands of residents were able to submit signatures and comments against the project. Then, the developer withdrew the project. Weeks later, that same developer moved the project to another county in North Carolina, where the closest neighborhood was predominantly Black and had a median income that was just one-third of the former community’s. Commissioners in the county quickly approved the project in a 6-1 vote. Who benefits from data center development? Even as data centers are more likely to be in communities of color, these same communities are less likely to receive major economic benefits, Thakur’s study found. Campuses operated by tech giants such as Meta, Google, and Microsoft are more likely to generate property-tax revenue and implement community benefit agreements, but those campuses are more likely to be in majority-white neighborhoods than communities of color. That pattern raises the prospect that communities of color are shouldering the financial and environmental burdens of data center development writ large without the same potential financial rewards, the researchers wrote. “A lot of the rhetoric coming from industry is that there are lots of economic benefits from data centers — tax revenue and job creation,” Thakur said. “These are what the industry groups promise, even though we’ve seen a lot of contradictions to that. But even if you do accept that as fact, the research shows that communities of color are less likely to receive those benefits.” According to some analyses, Black workers make up just 7% of AI workers compared to 13% of the general population. As for construction, for one week last fall, Capital B spent every morning and evening outside the site for Meta’s data center in northern Louisiana, the largest project in North America. The two closest towns are over 80% Black. None of the workers Capital B spoke to or saw drive off in their Ford F-150s were Black. As Black communities bear the brunt of this crisis, increasingly, they’ve also been left out of the imagined face of the opposition. Nationwide, roughly 70% of Americans opposed data centers. As such, the fight has been framed by advocates and politicians as one that crosses all racial and political boundaries. But researchers found that the flattening of data center opposition to an “American problem” has erased the racial injustices permeating the boom. Communities that have been highlighted via the media in resistance to data centers were about 79% white on average, compared with 53% white in communities without recorded opposition. They said that the disparity reflects unequal media coverage, political influence, and organizing resources. “It’s interesting that only some communities are being highlighted as opposing it,” Thakur said. “It is erasing the nuance and racial inequality” at the heart of the boom. At Capital B, we’ve highlighted Black communities fighting data centers everywhere from Memphis to Maryland and Mississippi. In Augusta, where the community closest to the massive data center site is 67% Black, residents are committed to fighting for a say. This summer, the board of commissioners approved a temporary moratorium on data center development. The $2 billion construction project was not included in the blockage. “We are asking for respect,” Mabery said.

items.originalTitle: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
items.author: Chantelle Lee
items.title: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
items.summary: Voting booths at a polling location inside Wayne Community College - Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Nov. 1, 2026. —Emily Elconin—Bloomberg/Getty Images Republicans and Democrats in several states engaged in a bitter fight to redraw congressional maps in their parties’ favor leading up to this year’s midterms. But in the aftermath of the blue wave that swept across the country, that conflict may be dying down—at least for now. Typically, maps are redrawn after the results of the U.S. census are released each decade, in order to account for population and demographic changes. Last year, however, President Donald Trump urged members of his party to redistrict mid-cycle ahead of the 2026 election as the GOP vied to hold onto its narrow House majority. Several Republican-led states moved to do so in the ensuing months, while Democratic leaders in other states responded with their own redistricting efforts, with varying degrees of success. The sweeping Democratic victories in the midterms, though, could mark a shift in the redistricting battle, political experts tell TIME. Read More: Are Democrats’ Stunning Midterm Upsets in Deep-Red States a Blip—or Is Their Map Expanding? Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, says that Republicans may be more reluctant to push for redistricting mid-cycle going forward, given that their efforts failed to counteract the blue wave in this year’s election . In states like Texas , North Carolina, Ohio , Alabama, and Florida , Democratic candidates came out on top in multiple districts that had been redrawn to benefit Republicans—which political experts have largely attributed to the fact that, despite redistricting efforts, Republicans were still facing a challenging political climate at a time when Trump’s approval rating was at a historic low . “In recent years, Democrats have been reluctant to engage in mid-cycle redistricting. Republicans have been more willing to do that, and Democrats have followed suit in response in order to counteract some of the districts created by Republicans to advantage themselves,” Panagopoulos says. “But as 2026 showed us, those efforts often amount to very little and can even backfire, so I think both parties right now are cautious about any mid-cycle redistricting efforts, and 2026 suggests that even if districts are very heavily gerrymandered to advantage one party or the other, there are no guarantees that those parties will win,” he continues. Mark Jones, a professor of political science at Rice University, says that, for Republicans, “pretty much anything that they could have done, they already did.” And he says that even if there are states where additional redistricting could in theory help make maps even more favorable for Republicans, GOP lawmakers will now face a challenging time pushing such legislation through if their power in the state governments was reduced—for instance, in Texas, where Democrats gained control of the state House and the governorship . Meanwhile, the Democrats who were advocating for redistricting in recent months were doing so as “defensive measures,” says Alvin Tillery, the director of Northwestern University’s Center for the Study of Democratic Governance and a Democratic pollster and consultant. And Jones says that, with the party’s sizable victories in this year’s midterms, “the sense of urgency” to redistrict “is no longer there.” It’s possible, Jones says, that some “unfinished business” may continue — for instance, Virginians passed a redistricting ballot measure in April, but the state Supreme Court prevented the newly drawn maps from taking effect; Jones says that Democrats could try to take up that effort again. But generally speaking, “I don’t think we’re going to see the gerrymander armed race in 2027 that we saw in 2025,” Jones says. If some of those efforts do proceed, he says, “I think it’s going to be at the margins.” “The Democratic Party reluctantly engaged in mid-decade redistricting only after Donald Trump and Republicans drew first blood, and given the size of the victory and the lesser the sense of urgency and need to bolster the number of seats that are safely Democratic, I think we’re going to see Democrats try to return to the norms that have governed U.S. politics in the modern era,” Jones says. That doesn’t mean that partisan gerrymandering has come to an end, experts point out. The next redistricting cycle will take place after the 2030 census, and Panagopoulos says, “When it’s a redistricting cycle, both parties engage to the extent that they can in partisan gerrymandering.” And Democrats, he says, “will remain better positioned to engage in pro-Democratic redistricting in part because of the gains that they made in state legislatures and governorships across the country.” “I don’t think redistricting is high on any party’s agenda at the moment,” Panagopoulos says. But, he continues, “Things will clearly shift in the aftermath of the 2030 survey, and what will be more important is what the partisan makeup of states and state legislatures looks like at that time.”

items.originalTitle: ‘Mississippi Snakes,’ decades in the making, offers a close look at these spellbinding reptiles
items.author: Jesse Yancy
items.title: ‘Mississippi Snakes,’ decades in the making, offers a close look at these spellbinding reptiles
items.summary: Authors Terry Vandeventer and Robert Young set out to unravel perhaps the most complex relationship between man and animal: that between man and snake. “Few people have a take ‘em or leave ’em attitude when it comes to their feelings regarding snakes,” the introduction to their book “Mississippi Snakes” reads. “Whatever feelings one may harbor about snakes, these emotions are often deep-rooted and intense.” Some people might consider these remarks understatements, which underscores the challenge Vandeventer and Young undertook in writing a book for “the masses” that offers a doorway to a greater understanding and humane treatment of these complex, fascinating creatures. The result is 400 pages of detailed, informed observation and analysis set out in a fluent, familiar style laced with wry humor and play. The book is superbly illustrated with photographs, drawings, and maps, and provides readers with authoritative, up-to-date information for the more than 50 kinds of snakes that make their home in the Magnolia State. The cover of “Mississippi Snakes.” Credit: University Press of Mississippi What’s more is “Mississippi Snakes” offers a fascinating, kaleidoscopic perspective on the people and culture of Mississippi from a snake’s-eye view, as it were. During over 30 years of field work, the authors met Mississippians of all stripes, “anglers, hunters, amateur and professional naturalists, farmers, country-store owners, foresters, and old bluesmen sitting on Delta porches,” who added their own beliefs and stories to the cultural narrative of snakes. This narrative is further enriched by snakes in story, song and notions derived from both the Old World and the New. A primary emphasis of “Mississippi Snakes” is on the identification and natural history of Mississippi snakes. Each profile of the over 50 species and sub-species of snakes in the state provides distinguishing characteristics (as well as common variants), a natural history that includes common names and their origins, habitat, distribution (with detailed state maps for each species), temperament, behavior, reproduction and whether the species is venomous or not. The identification of venomous snakes and the rare instances of snakebites are treated in separate sections, both of which implore the casual naturalist, hunter or fisherman to leave snakes alone. The authors point out that many snakebites are due to someone trying to kill or capture a snake, venomous or not. Though full of information, the species descriptions are shorn of the technical language and nuances of scholarly publications to make identifying snakes in the field fast and effortless. This reader-friendly style permeates the entire book and is a joy to read. As biologist William Lamar observes in his eloquent preface, Mississippi is “nothing if not a land of stories.” He continues, “The authors share with us the incomparable folklore surrounding its snakes, some of it partly based on fact or misunderstanding, with a tranche — like so much gossip — lodged firmly in the realm of fantasy.” In the Choctaw language, “‘sinti means ‘snake,’ while ‘sintollo’ is the word for ‘beloved snake’ and refers to all rattlesnakes,” the authors write to illustrate the differing perspective Native Americans had on the natural world. A cottonmouth figures prominently in “True Evil,” a novel by Mississippi author Greg Iles, and Faulkner describes his protagonist stepping on two “moccasins” while rescuing people from rooftops during the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927. Snakes often find their way into Mississippi blues, “literally or metaphorically,” among lyrics that “reflect love lost, rejection, unfaithfulness, and as is typical of most blues songs, a touch of risqué innuendo.” The authors offer samples in “Crawling King Snake,” “Cottonmouth” and “Black Snake Moan.” Snakes appear in the names of places throughout the state, such as the two Rattlesnake Creeks, one in Lauderdale County and another in Carroll County. The practice of snake handling receives a thorough, enlightening examination, and the Lake Washington “Snake Grabbin’ Rodeo,” during which harmless water snakes are caught and released, receives a nod. “Mississippi Snakes” reveals this diligence in every sentence. The scholarship behind this work is impeccable, the research comprehensive and thorough. “Mississippi Snakes” provides both professionals and the casual outdoorsman or backyard naturalist a concise, accurate field guide, and we have every reason to believe that the authors’ hopes of the book finding its way “into the college classroom as a definitive reference on Mississippi snakes” will be realized in short order. As for the authors’ other “grand dream,” that the book will “perhaps strike a spark in the curious mind of some youngster who will hopefully, someday, grow up to write an even better book,” that certainly might happen, but a better book than “Mississippi Snakes” will be a long time coming.

items.originalTitle: CT looks to next steps after ruling on ICE: ‘We’re not backing down’
items.author: Laura Tillman
items.title: CT looks to next steps after ruling on ICE: ‘We’re not backing down’
items.summary: A masked ICE agent enters the Meriden courthouse on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_3260-771x578.jpeg" /> The news last week that four provisions of a law intended to regulate U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement action in Connecticut were blocked by a federal judge was “not a surprise” to some immigration advocates. But, they argued, it didn’t erase the impact of state officials’ willingness to take action in the face of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. “I think it underlines our state, and especially our legislators’ willingness to still pass policies that could be challenged because they were the right thing to do, and send a message to residents — immigrant and non-immigrant — that is is where Connecticut stands,” said Constanza Segovia, organizing director for Connecticut For All and co-founder of Hartford Deportation Defense. She said when the laws were passed, including the provision that aimed to stop agents from wearing masks or other facial coverings when they interface with the public, advocates were aware there would be pushback. But Segovia, other advocates and some lawmakers said they are exploring the ways in which the state’s existing laws and new proposals that might come up in the 2027 legislative session can offer residents protection in response to safety concerns related to federal immigration enforcement actions. In the meantime, though, Carolina Bortolleto, an organizer with Greater Danbury Unites for Immigrants, said the ruling still “leaves Connecticut less safe” because “no one wants masked agents running around neighborhoods.” Senate Bill 397 was passed in 2026 and quickly was challenged by the U.S. Justice Department. The federal government called the law “blatantly unconstitutional,” saying that the state has no authority to tell federal agents what they can and cannot do. The government also argued that the law goes against the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which says that when state and federal laws clash, federal laws override those of the states. Judge Vernon Oliver agreed. The state law, Oliver wrote, “plainly imposes conditions on how federal officers must conduct and present themselves during the course of their federal duties, and it subjects them to criminal and civil penalties if they do not abide by those state-imposed conditions.” “But the Supremacy Clause ensures that federal operations are not chilled by state prosecution and that federal officers are immune from state prosecution when acting within the scope of their federal authority,” he added. ICE officials did not return a request for comment. Yet even in the wake of the decision, some immigrant rights advocates like Bortolleto were sounding a note of optimism. A provision of the bill that requires ICE agents to have a warrant in locations like schools, hospitals and places of worship remains in effect. “I think that’s really important because I think that section of the bill is what goes the longest way to making immigrant folks feel safer,” she said. Bortolleto said that she hoped that during the legislative 2027 session that begins in January, doctors’ offices could be added to the list of protected areas. Advocates also say that agents have frequently been observed wearing masks in the state even when that portion of the law was in effect. Miguel Castro, a member of the Meriden Middletown Immigration Alliance and second vice chair of the Connecticut Hispanic Democratic Caucus, noted the injunction is temporary and he still has hope that Connecticut will ultimately succeed. “Our state still has an opportunity to go back to the court process and challenge this as it is sits today,” he said. “It is a responsibility of the state under the 10th Amendment of the Constitution, using the sovereignty of our state, that it is our duty and fiduciary responsibility to protect the members of our community, and that’s what we intend to do.” Dealing with masked agents presents a variety of concerns, advocates say. “It’s a traumatic experience to see someone or a group of people with masks on, and they are carrying weapons, and you are by yourself and you have nothing to defend yourself with,” said Juan Fonseca Tapia, a co-founder of Greater Danbury Unites for Immigrants. “All you’ve got is a phone.” That phone can be used to record agents and provide evidence of abuses, but when those agents are masked, advocates say it can complicate accountability. The bill also sought to make officers wear identification, a provision that was blocked by Friday’s ruling. Segovia said it would be a priority in 2027 to look for regulatory loopholes that disenfranchise immigrants and people of color, and make sure they are closed. Supporting working-class immigrants means “supporting expansive healthcare policies that include everybody, regardless of immigration status,” Segovia said. Lawmakers should “make sure that nobody can touch our kids’ ability to go to public schools and public universities, regardless of their immigration status,” along with other key rights like renter protections. Segovia’s group is among those pressing the Lamont administration to put $10 million toward legal aid and emergency cash assistance for immigrants impacted by ICE enforcement. House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford said that he is interested in having that discussion in the new year. Ritter said the attempt to regulate ICE activity was worth pursuing, but ultimately there are “just limits to what the states can do.” He said it’s time for the Democratic majority in Washington to step up. “It’s not me throwing my hands up in the air saying, ‘we’re going to give up.’ We’re going to do everything we can to be helpful,” he added. “But there’s 259 Democrats in the House and 56 in the Senate, and if they need help learning how to pass bills I’m glad to go down there and try to help them.” Rep. Steven Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, a key backer of Connecticut’s law as co-chair of the legislature’s Judiciary Committee, said he was disappointed with the ruling. But “we’re not backing down,” he said. Stafstrom said there are still legal remedies to holding agents accountable for abuse of use of force. “One of the things that was blocked was having the inspector general do investigations into abuse of use of force, but just because that piece was inexplicably blocked, doesn’t mean Connecticut won’t continue to enforce state laws, it will just fall to individual states attorneys for the judicial districts to do that,” he said.

items.originalTitle: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
items.author: Kathryn Hughes
items.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
items.summary: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout.

items.originalTitle: ‘Beyond the Headlines’ Podcast: Reflecting on three years of Spotlight Delaware
items.author: David Stradley
items.title: ‘Beyond the Headlines’ Podcast: Reflecting on three years of Spotlight Delaware
items.summary: Allison Taylor Levine, Spotlight Delaware’s founder, CEO and publisher, joins the podcast for a special Thanksgiving week episode of “Beyond the Headlines.” Allison takes this moment to reflect with gratitude on almost three years of Spotlight Delaware journalism. She shares insights into the original impulses behind founding Spotlight, how the vision has played out in reality, and what she is looking forward to next in the journey. The podcast was hosted by Director of Community Engagement David Stradley. This transcript has been edited for length and clarity. Our editors are fond of asking: What’s the news peg for an article? Which means, what’s the recent event for the article that means the article needs to be written right now? The news peg for this interview is that last week, Spotlight Delaware hosted a screening of the Academy Award-winning film, Spotlight , about The Boston Globe’s investigative reporting team and its uncovering of the Catholic Church’s sexual abuse scandal. Before the screening, our chief operating officer, Matt Sullivan, interviewed you about the film’s connection to the origin of Spotlight Delaware. For those who weren’t there for that film screening, can you start by sharing how the origin story of Spotlight Delaware connects to the film Spotlight ? Absolutely. That film came out in 2015, which was just about the time I had been imagining some kind of potential … I wasn’t sure what it was yet, but some kind of a nonprofit newsroom, some kind of a solution for building up the local news ecosystem. I was doodling on the backs of napkins — wasn’t quite clear what I wanted yet. But, I was at the Knight Foundation conference in Miami that year, and they did a special screening of Spotlight . After the movie was done, they actually brought on stage the actual Spotlight team – the editor, who was Marty Baron, who was played by Liev Schreiber in the movie, and the reporters. I was just really very, very moved by the movie itself and by the stories that the reporters and that Marty Baron told after the movie. After seeing that and having that experience, I promised myself that if I ever had the opportunity to launch a nonprofit newsroom, that I would name it Spotlight Delaware, and we did. I didn’t realize your thinking about this had gone back all the way that far to 2015. Oh, yes. And before that, too, because like I said, I was sort of doodling on napkins by that time for probably four or five years at that point. I started going to this Knight Foundation conference in 2011, and that was a time when we talked about the connections between media and community, and I just started to get an inkling that we could do something to help build up the local ecosystem here. Although I really didn’t know what it was, and I didn’t have any resources. So I was just imagining at that time. The Boston Globe Spotlight team is specifically devoted to investigative reporting. Did you ever think about having Spotlight Delaware be solely focused on investigative work? Yes. And that was the original concept, based largely on what we heard from community listening. So that was where we started. I imagined us doing more longer-form stories that were not breaking news, and we did start like that. But that has evolved with the community’s needs and what the community has asked us to do. So now it’s a pretty different animal from where we started. But that was the original idea. As you watched the movie again, did anything resonate strongly with you or resonate differently with you now that you’ve been running Spotlight Delaware for three years? It was interesting to me. There’s a scene where Marty Baron goes to the publisher to essentially ask for permission to sue the Catholic Church for the needed records, and I realized when I was watching the movie that my role is now that of the publisher. Essentially, my job is to back up our editor-in-chief. If he comes to me and tells me there’s something important going on, then I need to listen to him and support him as much as I can. So that was an exciting moment. I’m not a journalism lifer. As I was prepping to take this job at Spotlight Delaware, I actually watched Spotlight . I come from the theater world, so I’m used to the people in that world being very passionate. The reporters in the movie Spotlight are very passionate and outgoing about it. I guess that surprised me. Seeing that passion, did you connect that back to how our staff operates? Oh, absolutely. I think our staff has that passion, has that energy. Our team kind of fits some of the stereotypes of the newsroom. You know, a slightly grumpy editor here and there. A very passionate young reporter here and there. The main character played by Mark Ruffalo, the main reporter, reminded me a lot of our Nick Stonesifer. And the reporter played by Rachel McAdams reminded me a lot of Maggie Reynolds, who covers our rural communities. It was exciting to see some of that energy and see the hustle bustle of the newsroom portrayed in the film and realize that it’s something that we have somewhat recreated here at Spotlight Delaware. One of the things I have learned about you and come to appreciate about you, Allison, is you are a very planful leader. You like making plans. You like managing to a plan. What has gone almost exactly according to plan at Spotlight in the three years? Well, I think we’re producing some great local news. That has gone according to plan. It’s a much bigger team than I expected, but I think the quality of the people and the vibe of the people – I love the way the people in our newsroom interact with the people in our whole organization. So that culture that we’ve created here is what I had hoped for and what I envisioned. And I think that our level of community engagement is also what I hoped for. I hoped that this would be a newsroom where we would hear from the community, we would talk with the community, and that the community would feel that they are a part of the newsroom. We will dive more into that later on. You talked about the team being bigger than you had imagined. What have been the biggest deviations from the plans that you made? I think Spotlight En Español is the biggest deviation. That was not the original plan to start a second brand. I’m really glad we did it, and I think it’s exciting work, and I think it’s something that is important to the community. I am not a Spanish speaker, so it was not something that I thought we were capable of pulling off. But silly me, I don’t have to do everything. We were lucky that we initially had José Ignacio Castaneda Pérez to help us get it off the ground, and now we have Cristal Sanchez and Nathaly Suquinagua helping us to keep that going, and I’m really proud of that work. But it is very different from what I imagined. Did not plan to do a bilingual news organization at all. Something else that wasn’t according to the initial plan is we launched arts and culture coverage two months ago at Spotlight Delaware. I came from a theater background. I remember when I came on, you were like, “David, we’re not going to write about arts and culture right away.” Can you talk, as an example of how Spotlight evolves and grows, about how that arts and culture work came to be the next thing for us? Well, it was always part of the dream, right? It was always part of the longer term vision, and we were talking about it from very early on, even before we launched Spotlight, that that would be part of it eventually. But we wanted to really get our legs under us first and make sure that we were doing a good job covering public policy issues, which we saw as the greatest need. Now that we have started to get our legs under us, we’re very excited to have Cannon Taylor here as our new deputy editor for arts and culture, and he’s just doing a great job telling some of the stories that are important to our community in the arts and cultural genre. I think that he’s doing a great job kind of digging out some of the unusual things going on, telling stories that go beyond the typical story about arts and culture, and I think that that is going to help Spotlight to grow our audience and grow our reach, as well as serve the community in different ways. A fraction of Delawareans are public policy wonks. But there are more people out there that are like, “Hey, I’m interested in something fun to do this weekend.” Absolutely. Yes. And we should be delivering both. When I moved to Delaware 20-plus years ago, I had just come from Vermont, and I was teaching a summer theater program in Vermont. There was this kid that every time we would do an improv exercise and ask for a setting, which we frequently do in improv, you ask, “Where should this scene happen?” This kid would go, “Delaware,” all the time. Finally, at the end of the summer, I asked, “Why do you always say Delaware?” And he just looks, and he sighs, and he goes, “Delaware is just so normal.” I think Delaware is more than normal. It’s awesome here. Exactly. And Cannon, as our arts and culture editor, definitely has an eye towards the weird. Some of Cannon’s writing about arts and culture would smash this child’s dreams about how normal Delaware is. And then what about surprises? What has surprised you the most so far in the three years of running Spotlight? I learned a lot about myself. I have never run a team before. I had only ever had one direct report before in my whole life, and usually that was a communications assistant type of role. I learned that, one, I’m good at hiring really good people, and that is an invaluable skill. And I have learned that I have to hire those good people and let them do their jobs and let go, which is, I think, very difficult probably for any leader. At first, you know, I wanted to copy edit everything. I wanted to read everything. I felt a lot of, and I still feel a lot of, personal responsibility, but that’s not pragmatic at all, and it is not necessary because I hire people and trust them to do their jobs. I started as director of membership and community engagement, and I remember being surprised just how quickly people were willing to give money to Spotlight Delaware. Yes! Even before you really started publishing articles, there was a really clear community need and desire for what Spotlight Delaware was going to be. The community response has been absolutely fantastic and tremendous, and you’re right, a bit of a surprise at how quickly it has built. I’m very grateful for that, and it is a clear indicator of the need in the community, and I think that it has grown as the community has seen us step up. W hat are some articles that stick in your head from the three years of Spotlight Delaware? I always point to the opioid series that Nick Stonesifer did, going back about 18 months now, and the huge impact that had on improving the grant-making process that the state runs to administer the opioid settlement funds. I also think of the tremendous work that Olivia Marble has done on covering the data centers in Delaware and how very early on Olivia reported on the initial hearing about one of the first data center projects in the state. As a result of her initial coverage, hundreds of people came out to that public hearing and many of them approached Olivia and said they were there specifically because of her coverage which made me really happy because part of our work here is about increasing civic engagement and, I think that that just illustrates the value of the work of reporting here. I’d like to talk about some jobs here at Spotlight Delaware, mainly your job and my job. One of your titles is publisher, and you talked about the scene in Spotlight where the publisher, you know, has the editor’s back. Can you tell listeners who may be not aware of the inner workings of a newsroom, what is the role of a publisher in a news organization? I think the role is different among different newsrooms. I don’t want to speak for all news organizations, but here, my role I think is really as the visionary, the strategist, and I like to say the storyteller-in-chief. I like to be the one who goes out and tells the story of Spotlight and what we’re trying to accomplish. And then I have two right hands. I have Jake Owens as our editor-in-chief, who runs the editorial side of the house, who works with the reporters and editors, and then Matt Sullivan who is running most of the business side of the house. My job is very often to play referee between the two of them. Sometimes those two sides of the house, there’s a tension between them, which is appropriate and important. But my role is to make sure that we are balancing our organizational sustainability with our journalistic responsibilities. I think a lot of people hear the title publisher and would think the publisher has a direct role in the news side of the operations. What is that interaction with the news team for a publisher? It’s very tricky. I don’t influence the stories that the editors and reporters select. Like any other person, any other Delawarean, I occasionally pitch a story idea here and there, hearkening back to my own days as a reporter. But it is incumbent on the editor-in-chief and on the reporters to take my idea like anybody else’s, and if it’s a good idea, great. If it’s not a good idea, ignore me. On the best days, ignore it. Worst days, they’ll just mock you openly to your face about the story idea. [Shared laughter.] Yes. That is true. And I welcome that, too! “ Oh, Allison, is this one of your idealist pieces about the power of community?” So, publisher — although you said the exact duties differ in organizations — is a fairly typical job in a news organization. Director of community engagement, my job, is not. When you were making your initial hires three years ago, you hired an editor-in-chief, two reporters, and then my position. Why was it important to you to have that community engagement role in place early on? Why not just hire more reporters? That was very intentional. Before we designed what Spotlight Delaware would look like, before we even knew we were going to launch a Spotlight Delaware, we did a six-month listening tour throughout the state to hear from people what they wanted, what they thought would be useful. They didn’t use this terminology, but they came back with essentially a collaborative, nonprofit, community-powered newsroom. And so to make sure that this newsroom is community-powered, we needed to make sure we were continuously centering community, and that’s why I thought one of our first hires should be someone really focused on that work, and I think that it has been really effective. I think most people that think about the beginning of a newsroom would not think about a community role in that. Yes, it’s a little different. Historically in newsrooms, there used to be a role called the ombudsman. Which is a much cooler title than director of community engagement. Well, we can talk about changing it, you know. But the ombudsman used to be the person who would engage with the community and interact with community members who had story ideas or concerns about stories. I think that the role of the director of community engagement is even more community-facing and more involved with the community, but there is some precedent for it. You did mention earlier that part of what has gone according to plan is the emphasis on community engagement. In your eyes, how have you seen that engagement work make an impact and play out in the trajectory here at Spotlight Delaware over the three years? Well, for one, it was the genesis of Spotlight Delaware en Español. We certainly would not have thought of starting Spotlight en Español if we hadn’t heard from the community that they wanted and needed it, so I think that’s one big way. We also hear a lot of story ideas from the community, and a lot of those story ideas do manifest into actual stories that our reporters and editors are producing. So I think that that is great because those stories are really a genuine, an authentic reflection of the community. So those are a couple of ways that I think it plays out. I have also noticed things like our reporters are constantly on Delmarva Public Media doing interviews. Not a month goes by that we don’t hear of a reporter being at somebody else’s event, running a panel or just showing up to talk about journalism. It feels like the reporters have taken that on themselves and say, “Hey, part of our job, even if we’re not reporting the news, is to be out there in the community.” Yes, absolutely. And that goes to the collaborative part of our work, I think, as well as the community-powered part of our work. But yes, it’s been great to see the reporters and the editors get as enthusiastic as they are about being in the community. I think that is good for the community. It’s also good for the reporters. It helps us to learn more about what’s happening in the community and what our community wants and needs. It helps the reporters also to build sources and meet people that they might not have met otherwise, which is enabling us to present a truer, more authentic reflection of the community. We’ve looked in the rearview mirror. Let’s look at what’s coming up. What are you most looking forward to in the next year at Spotlight Delaware? We have some exciting plans for growth in 2027 to continue to meet the community’s needs and to address the growing needs, and the community’s demands of us. Because as we have started to fill some of the gaps in the local news ecosystem, we are getting more and more requests from the community to do more and more. So I’m excited about those efforts, and I’m particularly excited to see our individual reporters grow because we are now just about to start our fourth year, and several of those reporters have been with us from very early on, and they are really growing. There’s three years in the past. Although you are very planful, you don’t have a three-year plan yet. But let’s jump three years forward. What would make you happiest three years from now about Spotlight Delaware? Oh, gosh. I would love to see Spotlight Delaware really serving the community in a larger way. I think that we have started to get our legs under us, and that we’re really starting to have an impact on the community. We are not reaching as many people as I want to yet, so I want us to continue to grow that audience and grow that reach. And, I’d love to see us break some additional stories that are very meaningful to our community. Well, it is Thanksgiving week. Let’s end with this: Looking back over three years of Spotlight Delaware, what are you grateful for? I am so grateful to this community for supporting Spotlight Delaware, and I’m really grateful that I took the chance. I’m glad that I took the leap. It was a big risk for me to leave my job at the Delaware Community Foundation, which I had had for 12 years, and I was very nervous about it. And I am just really grateful that I took a chance because now I get to run this wonderful organization and serve Delawareans in a different way. Well, I’m glad that when I asked you what would make you most happy in three years, your answer wasn’t, “I wouldn’t be running Spotlight Delaware anymore.” No, no. I want to stick around. Yes, please. Well, I am looking forward to the next steps of the journey, and thank you for coming on and sharing where Spotlight Delaware has been and where it’s going. Thank you, David. items.originalTitle: How woke Hollywood is remaking, and ruining, every film you've ever loved
items.title: How woke Hollywood is remaking, and ruining, every film you've ever loved
items.summary: The watchword for Hollywood these days isn’t "blockbuster" or even "star." It’s IP, or intellectual property. Left Coast moviemakers are overwhelming their audiences with regurgitated plots, characters and titles. It’s like a global sense of déjà vu, only we all know we have done it before. Think I’m joking? We just saw Robert Pattinson named the seventh movie-star James Bond (not counting the original "Casino Royale"). And HBO is working on a new "Harry Potter" series that’s scheduled to premiere on Christmas Day, just 15 years after we were done with the eight movies that made up the Daniel Radcliffe/ Emma Watson era of "Potter." The left hates author J.K. Rowling, but it sure is eager to remake her classics. It’s too early to tell how woke "Potter" will be, though producers have already created a furor by race-swapping the character Severus Snape in what one outlet said generated "months of 'woke' casting backlash." And given the original cast’s rejection of all things Rowling, I fear they will modify more to spite her and make news. REACTIONS POUR IN AFTER HBO DROPS NEW TRAILER FOR ITS UPCOMING HARRY POTTER MEGA-SERIES Sadly, that remake is hardly alone. The "Chronicles of Narnia" movies are also being remade, with Greta Gerwig’s new version, "Narnia: The Magician's Nephew," due out in February, about 17 years after the last movie debuted. It has already gotten bad reviews for casting Meryl Streep as the voice of the lion Aslan, who is supposed to be male because he’s also a Christ figure. And Hollywood is hard at work redoing the classic Hitchcock horror flick, "The Birds," of course changing the gender of the male lead to a movie "led by a new female protagonist," according to Deadline—with a far inferior director trying to outdo Hitchcock. DIRECTOR OF NEW ‘NARNIA’ MOVIE TAKES HEAT OVER CASTING OF MERYL STREEP AS CHRIST-LIKE LION ASLAN It’s all the intersection of greedy Hollywood and woke Hollywood. Greedy Hollywood will keep grinding out garbage because studios own the intellectual property. And woke Hollywood will keep making good shows and movies worse, deliberately disappointing more and more fandoms. Picture the three horrifying seasons of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" done to every good movie and TV show you’ve ever loved. In 2025, nine of the top 10 movies at the box office were either sequels or remakes, in some way trading on existing IP. In 2026, we’ve had a few more movies break through, but remakes and sequels still make up more than half the top 10. How long before they redo "Band of Brothers," with diverse casting, of course? ETHAN HAWKE BLASTS HOLLYWOOD'S 'GREEDY BASTARDS,' PREDICTS MASSIVE REBELLION AGAINST POWERFUL ELITES Yes, this isn’t new. Even the controversial silent film "The Birth of a Nation" had a sequel more than 100 years ago. The 1970s ushered in sequels for one of the most critically acclaimed movies of all time – "The Godfather." And that was followed by a tidal wave of science fiction film franchises like "Star Trek" and " Star Wars ." What we’re seeing now is different. It’s this endless cycle of books and graphic novels spawning movies, which in turn spawn TV shows, and perhaps new movies. The Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) shows how far off the rails this strategy can go. The original series had 23 movies, though many fans stopped with No. 22, 2019’s " Avengers : Endgame." 'THE MANDALORIAN AND GROGU' COLLAPSES IN SECOND WEEKEND AT BOX OFFICE, CEMENTING HUGE LOSS FOR DISNEY Disney didn’t stop there. Add 15 movies since then and 18 total series spanning 22 seasons, and you have a viewing public that doesn’t have a clue what is going on. But Disney didn’t like how poorly its recent woke movies were doing, so it is bringing back the very stars who made it all work. It’s even changing the ending of that entire series with an encore version of "Endgame." Meanwhile, you practically need AI just to watch it all and update you on the side plots. Hollywood producers are counting on each new release finding new fans and keeping some existing ones. That also means new merchandise, new spinoffs and more. Everything in the world becomes the MCU. Every beloved movie, TV show or book from your youth will now be executed (that’s the appropriate word) by someone with far less talent, style or skill. And, of course, with a far inferior cast. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION It’s a crisis so profound that famed director Steven Spielberg warned, "If all we make is known, branded IP, we’re going to run out of gas." He added: "There is nothing more important than giving the audience visual stories, and they can be in any form, but we need to tell more original stories." Clearly, nobody in Hollywood is listening to him. Movie fans might remember a Michael Keaton movie called "Multiplicity," where a man clones himself and each new clone becomes worse than the one before. That’s the strategy that has conquered Hollywood. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DAN GAINOR

items.originalTitle: Opinion: Montana’s ‘right to try’ law makes patients responsible for bearing costs — and risks
items.author: Skye A. Miner and Hannah O. James
items.title: Opinion: Montana’s ‘right to try’ law makes patients responsible for bearing costs — and risks
items.summary: In July, Montana became the first state to license clinics to offer patients who are not terminally ill drugs and devices that the Food and Drug Administration has not approved. Supporters call state Senate bill 535 a first-in-the-nation expansion of the “right to try.” Critics say it lets patients, including medical tourists from other states, pay out of pocket for unproven therapies. They are both right, in different ways. While the expansion of access to experimental treatments may provide patients with hope, the risks that patients may pay high costs for ineffective and even unsafe treatments remain high. The goal is to expand access to experimental therapies, with stem cell, anti-aging therapies, and biologics being likely use cases. But the law leaves major questions unanswered: How much will patients pay? Who will bear the cost if complications arise later? And, because these therapies are being used outside a rigorous research setting, how will anyone know whether they actually work? For patients, a primary concern is likely to be cost. SB535 makes patients financially responsible for the experimental treatment — with the price set by the company supplying the drug or device. The required patient agreement must describe “all the anticipated costs” of the treatment itself. But patients will likely face additional costs, including travel to Montana for those out of state, and follow-up care. Read the rest...

items.title: Why molecular cage catalysts show enormous differences in performance
items.summary: Chemistry researchers have developed a new way to identify and understand highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts using powerful "molecular cages" that mimic the behavior of nature's enzymes. These tiny, hollow molecular structures act like miniature reaction chambers to trap molecules and accelerate chemical reactions. The cages showed enormous differences in performance, with the best catalysts more than 10,000 times more active than the least effective ones.
